text: A presentation that starts with the owner’s pain, not with software.
Goal: $899 POS + tax and $7,500 restaurant Odoo ERP implementation
The owner has heard POS sales talk before. You need to sound like operations help.

Do not sell a terminal.
Diagnose business leakage.
The strongest negotiation position is created when the owner explains the cost of today’s broken process in their own words.
Your job: turn “software purchase” into “restaurant control system.”
What the restaurant owner is really thinking
Speak to their daily reality: staff, waste, mistakes, cash, time, and trust.
Can I trust my manager’s numbers?
Why does inventory not match sales?
How do I stop manual reconciliation?
Can I see the restaurant from home?
Move from curiosity → pain → value → commitment → implementation.
Preparation: build the business case before the pitch
Know what to observe before talking about price.
Owner view: sales, labor, inventory, purchasing, finance
Arrive with hypotheses. Leave with the owner’s numbers.
Opening script: disarm the sales reflex
The first two minutes must prove you are not rushing to sell.
“Before I show you anything, I want to understand how your restaurant actually operates. If our system does not solve enough problems to justify the investment, I will tell you.”
What is the biggest operational headache right now?
How are you handling it today?
How much time does it take each week?
What happens when somebody makes a mistake?
What do you think this costs every month?
Strategic silence: let the owner hear their own answer
Silence works after pain questions, price statements, and closing questions.
“Roughly what do you think that problem costs you every month?”
Do not rescue the owner from the pause. The pause is where the financial pain becomes real.
seconds of silence after a serious question
Calm silence says: “I am not desperate. I am thinking with you.”
Turn vague pain into measurable leakage
The owner’s own numbers make the investment feel logical.

The comparison is not $7,500 vs. nothing.
It is $7,500 vs. the cost of staying blind.
Demo a restaurant story, not random software screens
Show the owner what happens from order to business control.
Make the first decision simple and concrete.
Script: “The POS handles what happens at the counter.”
The ERP connects transactions to the rest of the business.

Low-stock alerts
Purchasing suggestions
Variance tracking
Owner view: sales, labor, inventory, purchasing, finance
Script: “The ERP handles what happens to the business because of those transactions.”
Leverage signals: read changes, not single gestures
Body language is a clue. Ask, don’t assume.
Asks “Can I see this from home?”
Use: “I noticed you spent more time on the inventory section. Is inventory control a major issue here?”
Objection handling: diagnose the objection before answering
Separate budget, value, risk, and decision-maker issues.
“Do you mean cash flow is difficult, or you are not yet convinced it creates $7,500 of value?”
“Then I would not replace it just because ours is different. What can’t you do with your current system?”
“Of course. What specifically would you like to think through?”
“I need to talk to my partner.”
“What do you think your partner’s biggest concern will be?”
Do not discount before you know which problem you are solving.
Pricing psychology: anchor against the cost of doing nothing
Use the owner’s leakage estimate to create financial context.
Say: “I would not compare $7,500 with spending nothing. I would compare it with what the current process is already costing the restaurant.”
Never promise full savings unless you can prove it. Keep the claim defensible.
Ask for blockers, then move to implementation details.
“Based on what we went through, is there anything important that would prevent you from moving forward?”
“Then let’s get the POS ordered and start the ERP discovery process.”
“Who should be the primary contact for menu data and restaurant operations?”
Show exactly what happens after the owner says yes.
Reinforce their own reasons: “We will keep coming back to the three goals you identified: inventory control, management visibility, and reducing administrative work.”
This turns the presentation into a practical business assessment, not a sales visit.
Owner view: sales, labor, inventory, purchasing, finance
Whether they buy today or not, give them something useful.

Don’t sell the POS.
Diagnose the restaurant.
When the owner sees the current process is already costing money every month, the POS + ERP becomes a business-control investment — not another tech expense.
Next action: schedule discovery → confirm scope → collect deposit → start POS + ERP setup
